sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Goroutines and channels are the features that made Go famous, and they appear in every Go fresher interview — often as the first 'can you explain concurrency in Go?' question. Even if you are interviewing for a role that does not write concurrent code, you will work in a Go codebase where goroutines are used for HTTP handler concurrency, background jobs, and timeouts. Understanding the fundamentals is non-negotiable.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Go's concurrency philosophy in one sentence: **do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.**

- **A goroutine is a lightweight thread managed by the Go runtime.** Not by the OS. Go multiplexes many goroutines onto a small number of OS threads. A goroutine starts with ~2 KB of stack (vs ~1 MB for an OS thread) and grows as needed. You can run tens of thousands of goroutines without running out of memory.
- **A channel is a typed pipe between goroutines.** One goroutine puts data in with `ch <- val`, another takes it out with `val := <-ch`. The channel synchronises the two — this is how you avoid shared-memory races for simple producer/consumer patterns.
- **Unbuffered channels synchronise; buffered channels decouple.** An unbuffered channel forces sender and receiver to meet at the same time. A buffered channel lets the sender proceed up to `cap` times before blocking.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Goroutine basics** — `go f()` launches `f` as a concurrent goroutine; `go func() { ... }()` for an anonymous goroutine; the main goroutine must wait or the program exits
- **Goroutine vs thread** — goroutines are scheduled by the Go runtime (M:N scheduling); much cheaper than OS threads; no explicit stack allocation needed
- **Channel creation** — `ch := make(chan int)` unbuffered; `ch := make(chan int, 5)` buffered with capacity 5
- **Buffered vs unbuffered** — unbuffered: both sender and receiver block until the other is ready; buffered: sender blocks only when buffer is full, receiver blocks only when buffer is empty
- **Send and receive operations** — `ch <- value` sends; `value := <-ch` receives; both are blocking by default (unless in a select with a default case)
- **Closing channels** — `close(ch)` signals no more values; receiving from a closed channel returns zero value and `false` for the ok: `v, ok := <-ch`; sending to a closed channel panics
- **Range over channel** — `for v := range ch` receives values until the channel is closed; the sender must close the channel to terminate the loop

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Main goroutine exits before child goroutines finish** — `go fmt.Println("hello")` followed immediately by `return` in main may print nothing. The program exits when main returns, killing all goroutines. Fix: use `sync.WaitGroup` or a done channel.
- **Sending to a closed channel panics** — closing a channel is a signal from sender to receiver. Only the sender should close. Closing a channel from the receiver side, or closing twice, panics.
- **Unbuffered channel deadlock** — `ch := make(chan int); ch <- 1` in the same goroutine with no other goroutine reading deadlocks immediately. The Go runtime detects this and panics with 'all goroutines are asleep — deadlock!'.
- **Goroutines are not free but they are cheap** — creating thousands is fine; creating millions may exhaust memory. The answer the interviewer wants: goroutines start at ~2 KB stack vs ~1 MB for OS threads, and are multiplexed by the Go scheduler.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"A goroutine is a lightweight function running concurrently — I start one with the `go` keyword. The Go runtime schedules goroutines onto OS threads using M:N scheduling, so goroutines start at about 2 KB of stack and I can run tens of thousands without issue. Channels are typed pipes I use to communicate between goroutines safely — unbuffered channels synchronise sender and receiver, buffered channels let the sender proceed without waiting. Go's design philosophy is to communicate through channels rather than sharing memory with locks, which makes concurrent code easier to reason about."*
